title: How should you open a case interview in the first two minutes?
description: The first three minutes set the tone. How to take notes, recap without repeating, and ask questions that actually help.
hook: The first two minutes of a case feel like the scariest part, because you have just heard a business problem for the first time and someone is waiting for you to speak. The good news is that these two minutes are also the most predictable. You listen, you say the problem back, and you ask a couple of sharp questions. Get this right and the rest of the case gets calmer.
body:
In this guide

  • Take notes that you can use
  • Recap the problem, not the paragraph
  • Ask at most three questions, and make them count
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Take notes that you can use

Split your page. Write the client's goal at the top, in a box, with any number and deadline attached ("$10M profit in 2 years"). Every answer you give later should connect back to that box. Put facts from the prompt on the left in shorthand, and leave the right side for your structure.

If you don't understand something, say so straight away: "Sorry, when you say margin, do you mean gross margin?" Faking understanding costs far more ten minutes later.

Recap the problem, not the paragraph

A recap shows you listened and lets you check the goal. Keep it to the client, the problem and what success looks like, in about three sentences. Never read the prompt back. Finish with a check: "Did I get that right?"

Ask at most three questions, and make them count

A good clarifying question changes what you draw next. If the answer wouldn't change your structure, don't ask it. The most useful questions are about:

  • The goal: is there a specific target and timeline?
  • The business model: how does the client actually make money?
  • The scope: are we looking only at this option, this country, this product?
  • The market: is the whole industry affected?

Then ask for time: "May I take a minute to structure my thoughts?" Silence while you think is fine once you've asked for it.

See it in action: Weak vs strong opening

Weak: "OK so the client is a telecom company in South-East Asia and they have revenue of $2 billion and it has fallen 6% and costs are flat and..." (reads the whole prompt back, asks five questions about the company's history).

Strong: "Our client is a mobile operator whose revenue fell 6% in a year while costs stayed flat, and we need to find out why and what to do. Is the rest of the market also declining? And do we know which part of the business is falling: contracts or pay-as-you-go?"

What to remember

  • Put the goal in a box at the top of your page.
  • Recap in three sentences, then check you have it right.
  • Only ask questions whose answers would change your structure.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. Which clarifying question is least useful?

  • Is there a profit target, and by when?
  • How many offices does the client have worldwide?
  • Is this happening to competitors too?
Show the answer

How many offices does the client have worldwide?. Unless the case is about offices, it won’t change your structure. The other two shape the whole case.

2. What should a recap include?

  • Every number in the prompt
  • The client, the problem and what success looks like
  • Your hypothesis for the answer
Show the answer

The client, the problem and what success looks like. Keep it short and check the goal. Hypotheses come after your structure.

Try it now

Prompt: "Our client is a UK gym chain with 50 sites. Membership revenue is up 5%, but profit has halved in a year. The CEO wants to understand why and fix it by next year." Recap it in three sentences or fewer, then write two clarifying questions.

Give yourself 2 minutes, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Recap: "A 50-site UK gym chain has growing revenue but profit has halved in a year. We need to find out why and fix it within a year. Is that right?" Questions: (1) "Is there a specific profit target for next year?" (2) "Are other gym chains seeing the same squeeze, or is it just us?" Optional third: "Has anything changed in the last year, such as new sites or a price change?"
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 2 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
